metadata.title: Gulf Stone Crab (Menippe adina)
metadata.source_file: Gulf Stone Crab SLH NOAA SEA.txt

nodes.title: TAXONOMY
nodes.body:
Common Name: Gulf stone crab
Scientific Name: Menippe adina

nodes.title: Classification
nodes.body:
Kingdom: Animalia
	Phylum: Arthropoda
	Class: Malacostraca
	Order: Decapoda
 	Family: Xanthidae

Note:	Reference for Scientific Name (768)
	Subphylum: Crustacea


Phylogeny: Menippe mercenaria has recently undergone systematic revision and was split into M. mercenaria and M. adina. Menippe adinia dwells along the western and northern portions of the Gulf of Mexico. It is assumed here that much of the biology will be similar between the species and only slight differences in seasonal matings, spawnings, habitats and behaviors may occur. It will take some time before these differences can be ascertained in the field and laboratory. Microhabitat distinctions between the species appears to occur. M. adina occurs both sub- and intertidally, whereas M. mercenaria is intertidal only in the hybrid zone (764).

Note: check above noted passage for correctness

nodes.title: VALUE & STATUS
nodes.body: Commercial:  The commercial importance of stone crabs comes from the meat of their chela and appears to be a relatively local phenomenon. The south of Florida is the major area of commercial importance with most of the crab claws being consumed in that same area without export. The same appears to be true of south Texas estuaries and fisherman, although some Texas claws are transported to meet increasing demand in Florida (Mark Tobb, per. comm.)

nodes.title: Indicator
nodes.body: Ecological Role: Stone crabs are assumed to be responsible for juvenile oyster mortality on oyster reefs.

nodes.title: GEOGRAPHIC RANGE
nodes.body:
Overall:  Wakulla County, Florida, west and south around Gulf of Mexico to Tamaulipas State, Mexico (768) .

Within Study Area: This species is common throughout the northern Gulf of Mexico with concentrated areas in south Texas estuaries.

Mobility and Migration:

nodes.title: Life Mode
nodes.body:
Eggs are maintained by the female beneath her abdomen until hatching. Larvae are planktonic. As they transform into juveniles, they settle out and are found in areas providing cover such as rubble and seagrass beds. Adults and juveniles are demersal, with adults often forming deep burrows in mud sediments. Juveniles usually do not form burrows, but use readily available crevices or existing cavities in close proximity to food. The stone crab has often been suggested as being nocturnal; however, there is equal activity at mid-day and mid-night which suggests a crepuscular activity cycle.

Migrations and Movements: Minor movements by the females from grass flats to deeper waters to avoid extreme temperatures have been noted. During the fall and winter, males appear to move from offshore areas to the grass flats for mating, and then back offshore (410 681)

nodes.title: BENTHIC HABITAT
nodes.body:
Habitat Type: All life stages are marine to estuarine.
Substrate: The gulf stone crab appears to require a substrate suitable for refuge, using either available cover or building burrows. It is found in rock or shell substrates, mud flats, grass meadows, and pilings. (FMP).

nodes.title: Physical/Chemical
nodes.body:
Temperature: In general, this species can tolerate waters ranging from 8O-32 C.  In cooler temperatures they often seal their burrows with mud (569). Larvae do not tolerate temperatures below 20 C, only being able to develop to the megalopae stage (522).

Salinity: They have low survival rates at low salinities (20-25 ppt) at 20 C; and do not survive in a salinity of 10 ppt. Megalopae are extremely sensitive to low salinity and extreme temperature (410). Adults are considered euryhaline although they are usually found in salinities close to seawater.

nodes.title: REPRODUCTION
nodes.body:
Reproductive Mode: Stone crabs are dioecious with mating taking place within a burrow or crevice (622). Mating is usually from November to March, sequenced with the spawning season (March to November, or possibly throughout the year in warmer climates such as Biscayne Bay and Florida Bay) .

Mating/Spawning: Sperm are stored by the female in the seminal receptacle, only a portion of the sperm are used at a spawning period, some maintained for later spawns. A female can spawn up to six times before mating again.

Fecundity: A single female can produce between 4-6 egg masses during a spawning season, averaging 4.5 spawnings per molt (111). Each sponge may contain 0.5-1.0 million eggs.

nodes.title: Length Range
nodes.body:
Egg: Fertilized eggs are maintained by the female until hatching, usually 9-14 days.

Larvae: Fastest growth was achieved in the laboratory at 30 C and 30-35 ppt, in which the megalopae stage was reached in 14 days and first crab stage in 21 days (522). Development of planktonic larvae to first crab stage usually requires 27 to 30 days, but may be altered by diet. They normally pass through five zoeal stages and then molt into megalopae.

Juvenile: Larvae metamorphose to juveniles at about 0.69 mg, no carapace dimensions are given. The smallest juveniles collected in the wild measure 1.4 mm carapace width (CW). at a size of about 35 mm CW, the carapace shape transforms to the adult shape. Juvenile growth is expected to cover 7 molts in 320 days and has intermolts of 40 days increasing in approximately 15 % increments per molt.

Adults: Males are heavier and gain weight faster than females (687). Terminal molts has been suggested to occur around 112 mm CW; while others have reached sizes of 130-145 mm CW. 30-35+ Carapace Width (CW).

nodes.title: FOOD HABITS
nodes.body:
Trophic Modes: Stone crabs appear to be entirely carnivorous at all stages of their lives.

Food Items: Larvae have specific dietary requirements apparently met by only certain types of planktonic animals. Juveniles fed on small mollusks, polychaete worms and crustaceans. Juveniles in captivity ate small bivalves, oyster drills, beef liver and chicken parts, polychaetes, and each other. Adults use their heavy chelae to crush all types of mollusks and are damaging predators on oyster beds. These crabs can exist up to two weeks without food after consuming a maximum of food (768 681 Bert et al. 1986).

nodes.title: ECOLOGICAL INTERACTIONS
nodes.body:
Competition:  Need information on competition.
Predation: Other than human, need information on predation.
Factors Influencing Populations: The Gulf of Mexico Fishery Management Council's Scientific and Statistical Committee recently (May 1990)(citation?) defined overfishing of stone crabs as occurring when crab claws are harvested at a size when the number of eggs/recruit is reduced below 70%. The fishery is well above the 70% level at present.

nodes.title: PEOPLE CONSULTED
nodes.body: Mark Tobb, Lu Belle's Seafood Brokerage, Port Aransas, Texas

Mating/Spawning: Sperm are stored by the female in the seminal receptacle, only a portion of the sperm are used at a spawning period, some maintained for later spawns. A female can spawn up to six times before mating again.

Fecundity: A single female can produce between 4-6 egg masses during a spawning season, averaging 4.5 spawnings per molt (111). Each sponge may contain 0.5-1.0 million eggs.

sections.heading: Length Range
sections.content:
Egg: Fertilized eggs are maintained by the female until hatching, usually 9-14 days.

Larvae: Fastest growth was achieved in the laboratory at 30 C and 30-35 ppt, in which the megalopae stage was reached in 14 days and first crab stage in 21 days (522). Development of planktonic larvae to first crab stage usually requires 27 to 30 days, but may be altered by diet. They normally pass through five zoeal stages and then molt into megalopae.

Juvenile: Larvae metamorphose to juveniles at about 0.69 mg, no carapace dimensions are given. The smallest juveniles collected in the wild measure 1.4 mm carapace width (CW). at a size of about 35 mm CW, the carapace shape transforms to the adult shape. Juvenile growth is expected to cover 7 molts in 320 days and has intermolts of 40 days increasing in approximately 15 % increments per molt.

Adults: Males are heavier and gain weight faster than females (687). Terminal molts has been suggested to occur around 112 mm CW; while others have reached sizes of 130-145 mm CW. 30-35+ Carapace Width (CW).

sections.heading: FOOD HABITS
sections.content:
Trophic Modes: Stone crabs appear to be entirely carnivorous at all stages of their lives.

Food Items: Larvae have specific dietary requirements apparently met by only certain types of planktonic animals. Juveniles fed on small mollusks, polychaete worms and crustaceans. Juveniles in captivity ate small bivalves, oyster drills, beef liver and chicken parts, polychaetes, and each other. Adults use their heavy chelae to crush all types of mollusks and are damaging predators on oyster beds. These crabs can exist up to two weeks without food after consuming a maximum of food (768 681 Bert et al. 1986).

sections.heading: ECOLOGICAL INTERACTIONS
sections.content:
Competition:  Need information on competition.
Predation: Other than human, need information on predation.
Factors Influencing Populations: The Gulf of Mexico Fishery Management Council's Scientific and Statistical Committee recently (May 1990)(citation?) defined overfishing of stone crabs as occurring when crab claws are harvested at a size when the number of eggs/recruit is reduced below 70%. The fishery is well above the 70% level at present.
